searches.title: Olof Rudbeck's Atlantica: Sweden as Atlantis
who: Olof Rudbeck (Olaus Rudbeck the Elder), professor of medicine at Uppsala
searches.method: A literary and linguistic argument. No survey, excavation or instrument work is described in the source I read.

announced.text: A four-volume, 3,000-page treatise argued that Sweden was Atlantis, the cradle of civilization, and that Swedish was the original language of Adam.
announced.where: book (Atlantica), published in volumes from 1679
announced.evidence: Between 1679 and 1702, Rudbeck dedicated himself to contributions in historical-linguistics patriotism, writing a 3,000-page treatise in four volumes called Atlantica where he purported to prove that Sweden was Atlantis

outcome.text: The argument was made from texts, so nobody ran a physical test. It was criticised by contemporaries, including the Danish professor Ludvig Holberg.
outcome.evidence: His work was criticized by several Scandinavian authors, including the Danish professor Ludvig Holberg

replies.who: Ludvig Holberg and other Scandinavian authors
replies.what: Criticised the work (Wikipedia names Holberg only; I did not read the criticisms themselves).

searches.notes: Source is Wikipedia only, so volume dates (1679 to 1702) are as Wikipedia gives them. I could not fetch a primary text of Atlantica or a library catalogue entry. A 1689 illustration from the book is described on the same page.

searches.title: Ignatius Donnelly, Atlantis: The Antediluvian World
searches.method: Comparison of ancient civilisations and myths across the Old and New Worlds (hyperdiffusionism, per Wikipedia). No sea-floor work.

announced.text: Atlantis was real, was a large island in the Atlantic and the source of all later civilizations, and the Azores are its remnant.
announced.where: book (Harper & Brothers, New York)
announced.evidence: There once existed in the Atlantic Ocean, opposite the Mediterranean Sea, a large island, which was the remnant of an Atlantic continent, and known to the ancients as Atlantis.

outcome.text: Swedish oceanographer Hans Pettersson argued in 1944 that no island in the Atlantic could have sunk in the time Plato gives, because continents do not sink and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is building volcanic crust. Plate tectonics later became accepted.
outcome.evidence: Thus, there never was a larger island in the Atlantic which sank.

replies.what: Wrote 'Die Atlantislitteratur unserer Zeit: Betrachtungen eines Geologen' against the geological case for an Atlantic Atlantis (as described by Franke's page, not read directly).
Atlantis och Atlanten: argued no sunken Atlantic land fits Plato's date.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Plate tectonics and sea-floor geology: the ridge is erupting crust, not sinking land (Pettersson's argument, 1944).
searches.notes: The refutation source is Franke's Atlantis-Scout page, a scholarly but individual website that summarises Pettersson. I did not read Pettersson's 1944 text.

searches.title: Termier's Atlantis lecture and the Azores lava glass
searches.method: Examination of a piece of volcanic glass (tachylite) hauled up in 1898 during cable work, to ask whether the sea floor there had once been dry land.

announced.text: Termier argued the tachylite could only have cooled to glass in air, so the sea floor it came from was land not more than about 25,000 years ago.
announced.where: lecture, 1913
announced.evidence: he concluded that the sea floor from which the tachylite came once lay above water... this happened not more than 25000 years ago since the sea water affected the lava's surface only little

outcome.text: Högbom said in 1938 that lava can cool to glass under water, and that rocks rafted by Ice Age icebergs to the Azores all settled near today's coast, which means land and sea levels there have been about the same since the last Ice Age. Pettersson adopted both points in 1944.
outcome.evidence: The rocks which were transported by icebergs during the ice age to the Azores all settled down near today's coast line. This means that the level of land and sea since the last ice age was approximately the same as it is today.

replies.what: Judged Termier too credulous; lava can form glass under water.

searches.check_that_settled_it: An already published explanation of the lava glass, plus iceberg-rafted rocks that mark the old shoreline at today's level.
searches.notes: All details come from Franke's summary of Pettersson. I did not read Termier's lecture, Högbom's 1938 paper or the cable-work report. The legends.json Azores entry says cores show the plateau has been underwater; I did not find a primary source for drilling in this lane (see not_verified).

searches.title: K. T. Frost: the Critias and Minoan Crete
searches.method: Literary argument, reading the Critias against what was then known of Minoan civilisation. No fieldwork.

announced.text: Plato's Atlantis story is best understood as a memory of Minoan Crete. A first version of the idea dates to 1909, according to Colavito.
announced.where: paper, Journal of Hellenic Studies 33 (1913)
announced.evidence: The attempt to answer these questions involves a consideration of the truth of Solon's visit to Egypt, a review of the whole problem of Atlantis and a glance at the relationship between Solon, Plato, and Critias.

outcome.text: The identification is a literary argument, and I found no survey or excavation reported as a test of it as Atlantis. Plato puts the island in the Atlantic and 9,000 years before Solon, which Crete does not match.
outcome.evidence: nothing has been added to it since Frost's academic version of the argument in his 1913 journal article following up on his 1909 proposal

sources.title: Jason Colavito, review of Atlantis Rising (2017)

searches.notes: I read only the Crossref abstract, which does not itself say 'Minoan Crete is Atlantis'; the title and Colavito's description carry that. The 'Crete matches Plato' reading is the one named in our legends.json entry.

searches.title: Bigelow and Iselin's Azores cruise on the ketch Atlantis
searches.method: A 42-day research cruise to study currents, with sounding and sampling gear also meant to probe the sea floor for signs of the 'Atlantean Plateau'.

announced.text: Newspapers reported that scientists would probe for Atlantis on the cruise; the scientists' stated aim was to study large currents.
announced.where: press (Minneapolis Sunday Tribune, October 1931) and WHOI history article
announced.evidence: scientists plan to probe for Atlantis by breaking through a thin submarine crust under which the legendary land is declared to be hidden.

outcome.text: The crew found nothing and made no claim.
outcome.evidence: the crew returned home empty-handed.

searches.check_that_settled_it: A sea-floor sampling cruise: nothing found; no published finding of land-surface rock.

sources.title: WHOI, 'How a newly established oceanographic institution in Woods Hole searched for the lost city of Atlantis'

searches.notes: The WHOI page frames the Atlantis search as a side aim of a currents cruise. The quoted newspaper line is the Tribune as quoted by WHOI, not seen directly.

searches.title: Marinatos: volcanic destruction of Minoan Crete
searches.method: A reading of Minoan palace destruction layers across Crete, proposing one volcanic cause.

announced.text: The Minoan palace catastrophes on Crete were contemporaneous and caused by the Thera eruption. The abstract does not mention Atlantis.
announced.where: paper, Antiquity 13 (1939)
announced.evidence: Everywhere the catastrophes are seen to be contemporaneous.

outcome.text: The Antiquity editors added a postscript saying the evidence was insufficient for the claim that the eruption destroyed Minoan civilisation, and the hypothesis has since been rejected as stated. The eruption itself is real; Marinatos then dug Akrotiri.
outcome.evidence: The editors of Antiquity appended a postscript to his 1939 publication about the Thera eruption, stating that they believed the evidence currently insufficient to support Marinatos's hypothesis that the eruption had destroyed Minoan civilisation.

replies.what: Postscript doubting the evidence (reported by Wikipedia; I did not read the postscript).

searches.check_that_settled_it: Excavation of Akrotiri from 1967 and radiocarbon dating of the eruption (2006).
searches.notes: Our legends.json says later writers tied the eruption to Plato. Marinatos's 1939 abstract does not itself name Atlantis, so this entry is a turning point in the Thera story, not an Atlantis claim by Marinatos. I read only the abstract.

searches.title: Pettersson's geophysical case against an Atlantic Atlantis

place.name: Atlantic Ocean, Azores and Mid-Atlantic Ridge

searches.method: Review of the geology of the Atlantic, land-bridge theories, the Azores plateau and the 1913 Termier claim, against Plato's date.

announced.text: No Atlantic land could have sunk in the last ice age or since; continents do not sink, and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is erupting new crust.
announced.where: book (Atlantis och Atlanten, 1944)
announced.evidence: Continents do not just sink, too, as can be seen e.g. in the lack of deep ocean sediments on land, they only move horicontally on the earths surface.

outcome.text: Franke notes that continental drift was accepted only in the 1960s and 1970s, which supports Pettersson's reasoning. I read no later paper in this lane.
outcome.evidence: the theory of continental drift ... was accepted only very late, namely in the 1960s and 1970s.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Plate tectonics: no sunken Atlantic continent, and the Azores sit on volcanic ridge crust.
searches.notes: Secondary summary only; Pettersson's book was not available. Franke's own phrasing 'sufficiently evidenced' is his judgement.

searches.title: Mavor's search for Atlantis off Thera
searches.method: Underwater survey from a small boat off Thera, looking for a drowned Minoan town.

announced.text: WHOI says Mavor and colleagues found evidence of a Minoan city, and that the site seemed to mirror Plato's account.
announced.where: WHOI history article (the 1966 announcement itself was not read)
announced.evidence: Off the coast of the island Thera in the Aegean Sea, Mavor and fellow researchers found evidence of a Minoan city dating to 1,400 B.C.E.

outcome.text: WHOI says a long dispute over credit left the findings in doubt. The best-documented Minoan town on Thera, Akrotiri, was found by land excavation from 1967 and dated to the 16th to 17th century BCE.
outcome.evidence: years of disputing over who deserved credit for the discovery left Mavor's findings mired in doubt and skepticism among the public.

searches.notes: Only the WHOI summary, written decades later, and it gives a 1,400 BCE date that differs from the later radiocarbon range for the eruption (1627 to 1600 BCE, Friedrich 2006). I did not find Mavor's book or contemporary reports.

searches.title: Akrotiri excavations on Thera begin
searches.method: Land excavation of a Bronze Age town buried by pumice and ash, following up Marinatos's volcanic hypothesis.

announced.text: Marinatos's choice of the site paid off within hours: a buried Minoan town with frescoes was found.
announced.where: excavation reports and Wikipedia summary
announced.evidence: Marinatos's choice of the site proved to be correct and a few hours into the excavation, the remains of the buried city began to be discovered.

outcome.text: The town is real and was destroyed in the Theran eruption in the 16th century BCE per Wikipedia; radiocarbon work gives 1627 to 1600 BCE. That is about 8,000 years after Plato's date, and the site is inside the Aegean. It confirms a real buried town, not Atlantis.
outcome.evidence: The settlement was destroyed during the Theran eruption sometime in the 16th century BC, and was buried in volcanic ash, which helped preserve its fine frescoes.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Excavation and dating: a real town, wrong date and wrong place for Plato's story.
searches.notes: Coordinates 36.35139 N, 25.40361 E are from the Wikipedia Akrotiri page, which I fetched. 'About 8,000 years' is my arithmetic (9,600 BCE minus about 1,600 BCE).

searches.title: Bimini Road found; Cayce's Atlantis readings
searches.method: Diving observation in 5.5 m of water off North Bimini. Edgar Cayce's 1930s trance readings had already named Bimini as a mountaintop of Atlantis.

announced.text: Divers reported a pavement of rounded stones that they thought might be man-made, which became known as the Bimini Road.
announced.where: dive report; Valentine, Muse News (Miami Museum of Science), 1969
announced.evidence: On September 2, 1968, while diving in 5.5 meters (18 feet) of water off the northwest coast of North Bimini, Joseph Manson Valentine, Jacques Mayol and Robert Angove encountered what they called a "pavement"

outcome.text: Geologists who studied it found beachrock jointed into blocks. See the 1977 to 1980 coring and dating entry.
outcome.evidence: The consensus among geologists and archaeologists is that the Bimini Road is a natural feature composed of beachrock

searches.check_that_settled_it: Coring and radiocarbon dating of the stones, plus the geology of jointed beachrock.
searches.notes: Coordinates from the Wikipedia Bimini Road page. Wikipedia says Cayce's readings described Bimini as 'a mountaintop of Atlantis' in 1931 coverage. I did not read the 1969 Valentine article.

searches.title: Soviet photographs of a 'wall' on Ampère Seamount

place.name: Ampère Seamount, Atlantic, about 410 km SW of Portugal

searches.method: Underwater photography on the shallow summit (a 6 by 3 km plateau at about 120 m, with a peak at 55 m).

announced.text: Photographs seemed to show cut blocks and steps on the summit, which led to Atlantis speculation. Aksyonov publicised the photos in 1979 and thought the stones had stood on dry land, but did not himself call them Atlantean.
announced.where: press, 1979 (New York Times, 21 May 1979 is cited by Wikipedia; not read)
announced.evidence: Underwater photographs taken during this expedition revealed a stone wall which included cut stone blocks scattered on both sides... This was the grounds for speculation that it may have been the location of the legendary Atlantis.

outcome.text: Atlantipedia says that when better images were obtained, Aksyonov declared the features natural. This rests on a secondary and fringe-friendly site.
outcome.evidence: a couple of years later when better quality images were obtained, Akysonov declared that the original features were natural, ruling out an Atlantean explanation.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Better-quality photographs of the same features (as reported by Atlantipedia).
searches.notes: Coordinates 35 04 N, 12 57 W from the Wikipedia page. I could not open the 1979 NYT article (blocked) or the 'Atlantis Rising' article Atlantipedia cites, so the natural-features outcome is second-hand. Ampère Seamount is not in our 15 places; suggest the hypotheses lane add it.

searches.title: Cores and dating of the Bimini Road
searches.method: A core from the stones taken in 1977 and radiocarbon dated at the University of Miami, uranium-thorium dating of the limestone under the stones, and field description of the blocks.

announced.text: Proponents held the stones were a worked road or wall. Cores from the stones gave seven radiocarbon ages between 2,750 and 3,510 radiocarbon years BP, on whole rock, shells and cement, and the stones are beachrock.
announced.where: Calvert, Introne and Stipp, Radiocarbon 21 (1979); McKusick and Shinn, Nature 287 (1980)
announced.evidence: dated as whole rock and in separated components of shell material and cement, to determine maximum age of "road-like" formation.

outcome.text: The published consensus is natural beachrock broken by joints. Proponents argued the dates came from whole-rock samples open to young carbon; Wikipedia says the background data show not all were whole-rock.
outcome.evidence: The consensus among geologists and archaeologists is that the Bimini Road is a natural feature composed of beachrock that orthogonal and other joints have broken up into roughly rectangular, polygonal, and irregular blocks.

replies.what: Shinn, 'A Geologist's Adventures with Bimini Beachrock and Atlantis True Believers', Skeptical Inquirer 28 (1).
Published a rebuttal of the beachrock report (title as cited by Wikipedia; not read).
'Bahamian Atlantis reconsidered', Nature 287.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Radiocarbon dates of the stones (2,750 to 3,510 radiocarbon years BP, not calibrated) and the beachrock geology.

sources.title: Calvert, Introne and Stipp, 'University of Miami Radiocarbon Dates XIV', Radiocarbon 21 (1979)
Crossref record, McKusick and Shinn, Nature 1980
Crossref record, Harrison, 'Atlantis Undiscovered - Bimini, Bahamas', Nature 1971

searches.notes: The Christian Science Monitor piece 'Another Atlantis myth exploded' (24 September 1980) appears in search results, but my fetch returned no article text, so I did not use it. I saw only titles for the Nature items. Uranium-thorium date on underlying limestone, 14,992 +/- 258 BP, comes from Gifford and Ball via Wikipedia. Corrected 2026-11-11 from the table printed in Radiocarbon 21: UM-1359 whole rock 2780 ± 70, UM-1360 3500 ± 80, UM-1361 3350 ± 90, UM-1362 shells 3510 ± 70, UM-1363 cement 2750 ± 80, UM-1364 2770 ± 80, UM-1365 2840 ± 70. Wikipedia's Bimini Road article, used before, gives UM-1362 as 2780 and UM-1365 as 2770 (research/atlantis/evidence/bimini-road.md).

searches.title: Sonar images of structures off western Cuba (ADC survey)
who: Manuel Iturralde (Cuban Natural History Museum geologist)

place.name: Off the tip of the Guanahacabibes Peninsula, Cuba, more than 650 m deep

searches.method: Sonar during a survey for sunken Spanish ships, in a joint venture with the Cuban government, then (per Ancient Origins) a July 2001 return visit with an ROV and video.

announced.text: The company said it had found stone structures that might be a drowned city. Zelitsky declined to name them until there was evidence, and did not link them to Atlantis.
announced.where: BBC News Online and Globe and Mail, 7 December 2001
announced.evidence: "It's a really wonderful structure which really looks like it could have been a large urban centre," ADC explorer Paulina Zelitsky told the Reuters news agency. "However, it would be totally irresponsible to say what it was before we have evidence."

outcome.text: Experts quoted at the time were cautious and no published follow-up survey was found in the 2014 summary I read. Critics noted the depth, about 650 m, is far below any Ice Age sea level.
outcome.evidence: there have been no reported follow-up investigations and news outlets have gone deathly silent on the matter.

replies.what: "If I had to explain this geologically, I would have a hard time." (as quoted by Ancient Origins from National Geographic News, 28 May 2002; the NatGeo page would not load)
Depth is the main problem: Ice Age sea level fell about 100 m, not 600 m.

sources.title: BBC News Online, 'Lost city found beneath Cuban waters', 7 December 2001 (copy on CubaNet)
Globe and Mail, 7 December 2001 (copy on CubaNet)
Ancient Origins, 'What happened to the sunken city of Cuba?' (2014)

searches.notes: BBC says the team first spotted the structures 'last year' (2000); Ancient Origins says 2001. The Globe and Mail says 'may be a 6,000-year-old city'; Weinzweig is quoted there saying 'nobody has suggested they are natural'. No coordinates are given in these sources. The 2014 summary is secondary, so 'no follow-up' is as of its date. Not one of our 15 places.

searches.title: Collina-Girard proposes Spartel Bank
searches.method: Reconstruction of the Ice Age shoreline of the Strait of Gibraltar from sea-level and sea-floor depth data, as summarised by Wikipedia; I did not read the paper.

announced.text: At the ice-age low a 14 by 5 km island stood off Cape Spartel, in a sheltered sea 77 km long. The rising sea drowned it for good about 11,300 years ago.
announced.where: his open follow-up article (2002) to the 2001 paper in Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences
announced.evidence: formait alors une île (14 km de long sur 5 km de large)

outcome.text: A Bryn Mawr Classical Review (2009) of his book found real prehistory but not Atlantis. Gutscher, who mapped the bank, later said it could not have supported Plato's Bronze Age society.
outcome.evidence: he "has certainly succeeded in throwing some light upon some momentous developments in human prehistory in the area west of Gibraltar. Just as certainly, however, he has not found Plato's Atlantis."

replies.what: Bryn Mawr Classical Review of Collina-Girard's book L'Atlantide retrouvée?, noting date discrepancies and coincidences.

searches.check_that_settled_it: A multibeam map and habitability review (Gutscher, 2005) showed a small island and no settlement; reviewers noted date and size mismatches.
searches.notes: Crossref gives August 2001; Wikipedia says September 2001. Coordinates are from the Wikipedia Spartel page. I could not read the paper or the BMCR review directly. Wikipedia also says Georgeos Díaz-Montexano published a Spartel proposal in April 2000 (not read). Corrected 2026-11-11 from his 2002 article: an earlier version of this entry, from Wikipedia's summary, gave an island 10 to 12 km across drowned by meltwater pulse 1A around 9400 BCE. The article has the sea at -55 m at 11,300 years ago, which it calls meltwater pulse 1B, and puts pulse 1A at about 14,000 years ago (research/atlantis/evidence/spartel-bank.md).

searches.title: Gutscher's survey and earthquake test of the Spartel Bank
searches.method: High-resolution multibeam bathymetry of the paleo-island, plus Gulf of Cádiz tsunami and turbidite records, to test whether a great earthquake and tsunami could have sunk it.

announced.text: A great earthquake and tsunami like 1755 could explain a sudden sinking about 11,600 years ago, and an unusually thick turbidite about 12 ka may fit. The bank's shape and the case for human habitation were reported.
announced.where: paper, Geology 33 (2005) 685 to 688
announced.evidence: An unusually thick turbidite dated as ca. 12 ka may coincide with the destructive event in Plato's account. The detailed morphology of Spartel paleoisland, as determined from recently acquired high-resolution bathymetric data, is reported here.

outcome.text: In follow-up correspondence Gutscher said the island could not have been Atlantis, since Spartel could not have supported the Bronze Age society Plato describes.
outcome.evidence: In follow-up correspondence, however, Gutscher indicated that the island could not have been Atlantis, referring to Plato's description of a Bronze Age society, which Spartel could not have supported at the time.

replies.what: BMCR: not Plato's Atlantis (reviewing Collina-Girard).

searches.check_that_settled_it: The multibeam map: a small island, with no evidence of a city, and Gutscher's own later statement.
searches.notes: The survey years 2003 to 2005 come from the task brief. The abstract says only 'recently acquired'. I found Gulf of Cádiz cruises (R/V Sonne SO175, November to December 2003; Le Suroît, 2004 and 2005) in a search result but could not tie them to Spartel, so they are not used. The Gutscher statement is as reported by Wikipedia citing an archived ThoughtCo page; I did not read it.

searches.title: Kühne and Wickboldt: rings in satellite photos of the Doñana marshes

place.name: Marisma de Hinojos, Doñana, near Cádiz

searches.method: Visual inspection of satellite photographs for rectangles and ring shapes in the mud.

announced.text: Satellite photos of the Marisma de Hinojos show two rectangles and parts of concentric rings that Kühne reads as Plato's temples and ring system. Wickboldt first spotted them.
announced.where: Antiquity Project Gallery (online), reported by BBC News 6 June 2004
announced.evidence: "We have in the photos concentric rings just as Plato described," Dr Kuehne told BBC News Online.

outcome.text: The Spanish Hinojos Project later worked in the same marsh. It found a settlement about 5,000 years old under metres of sediment, which is a different date from Plato's, but I found no published test of the specific rectangles and rings.
outcome.evidence: It is not known if any of these shapes are natural or manmade and archaeological excavations are planned.

replies.what: "What we need here is a date range. Otherwise, you're just dealing with morphology." He also said "you've got several leaps of faith here."

sources.title: BBC News, 'Satellite images show Atlantis' (Rincon, 6 June 2004)
Crossref record, Kühne, Antiquity Project Gallery 2004

searches.notes: I did not open the Antiquity page itself. BBC says the sizes in the photos are slightly larger than Plato's and gives two explanations, including a 20% longer stade. No coordinates in the BBC article.

searches.title: Sarmast's expedition and the 'Atlantis' hill off Cyprus

place.name: Cyprus Basin, about 80 km off southeast Cyprus, about 1.5 km deep

searches.method: Deep-water side-scan sonar from a ship, read as a walled hill, a 3 km wall and trenches.

announced.text: Sarmast said his team had definitely found Atlantis. At the news conference in Limassol he showed only animated simulations of the hill.
announced.where: news conference, Limassol, Sunday 14 November 2004 (Reuters, 15 November)
announced.evidence: "We have definitely found it," said Sarmast... "We cannot yet provide tangible proof in the form of bricks and mortar, as the artifacts are still buried under several meters of sediment, but the circumstantial and other evidence is irrefutable," he claimed.

outcome.text: A German geophysicist and others said the feature was a mud volcano or natural salt-tectonic fold. Later published surveys by Hübscher and colleagues described a natural compressional fold and a slide scar.
outcome.evidence: the features that Sarmast interprets to be Atlantis consist only of a natural compressional fold caused by local salt tectonics and a slide scar with surficial compressional folds at the downslope end and sides of the slide.

replies.who: A German physicist and two other scientists (not named by Cyprus Mail)
replies.what: Said it was a 100,000-year-old mud volcano and that they had surveyed the same area the year before.
"the real killer of the hypothesis is that 100,000-year-old mud volcanoes exist on the spot."
Said it was a 'table top mountain', not a mud volcano, and challenged critics to prove their claims.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Published multibeam and seismic work on salt tectonics and mud volcanoes in the Cyprus Basin, and the age of the basin sediments.

sources.title: Cyprus Mail, 'Another scientist casts doubt on Atlantis theory', 20 November 2004
Wikipedia, Location hypotheses of Atlantis (Cyprus section)

searches.notes: The Hübscher result is as described by Wikipedia; I confirmed the paper's title and journal through Crossref but saw no abstract. Wikipedia also says the Mediterranean last dried 5.59 to 5.33 million years ago, so there was no Ice Age dry land there. Sarmast published a book in 2006.

searches.title: Spanish Hinojos Project in the Doñana marsh
who: CSIC, Universities of Huelva, Granada and Barcelona, FUHEM

place.name: Marisma de Hinojos, Doñana National Park

searches.method: Boreholes through the marsh sediments, with pollen and microscopic traces of human and animal activity, geological and chronological dating.

announced.text: The marsh was inhabited about 5,000 years ago by farmers and herders. A marine flood between 2200 and 2000 BCE, coinciding with a Gulf of Cádiz tsunami, ended that community. Further Atlantic tsunamis followed around 1450 BCE and about 300 years later.
announced.where: CSIC press release, 13 November 2018, on a paper in Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports
announced.evidence: La marisma de Hinojos, en el Espacio Natural de Doñana, estuvo poblada hace 5.000 años. (The Hinojos marsh in the Doñana Natural Space was inhabited 5,000 years ago.)

outcome.text: The release does not mention Atlantis. It dates a real settlement in the marsh to the third millennium BCE, more than 6,000 years after Plato's date. It also says the coast sank progressively until the first centuries CE.
outcome.evidence: Este episodio geológico, que coincidió con un tsunami en el Golfo de Cádiz, puso fin repentino a esa comunidad y a su cultura (This geological episode, which coincided with a tsunami in the Gulf of Cádiz, brought a sudden end to that community and its culture)

searches.check_that_settled_it: Coring and dating: a third-millennium BCE settlement buried under metres of sediment, on a coast that was inland sea until recently.

sources.title: CSIC press release, 'Halladas pruebas de poblamiento humano durante la prehistoria reciente en las marismas de Doñana' (13 November 2018)

searches.notes: Translations are mine. The release says the project started in 2005 with support from the Doñana Biological Station of CSIC. I did not read the journal paper, so the quoted numbers are the press release's. The marsh is where Kühne (2004), Freund (2011) and Merlin Burrows (2018) placed Atlantis.

searches.title: Milos conference and the 24 criteria
searches.method: A three-day international conference of speakers holding competing theories; a majority supported a list of 24 criteria a candidate site must meet.

announced.text: A list of 24 criteria, including: outside the Pillars of Hercules; alternating concentric rings of land and water; sunk entirely or partly; destroyed 9,000 Egyptian years before the 6th century BCE; elephants present; hot and cold springs; black, white and red rocks.
announced.where: conference conclusion, proceedings edited by S. Papamarinopoulos
announced.evidence: The conference concluded with agreement on a list of 24 criteria, which any proposed site must meet to qualify as a site where Atlantis could have existed

outcome.text: No site has been shown to meet the list. The Atlantipedia author calls its main flaw the assumption that all of Plato's account is factual, and Jim Allen expanded it to 50 points and used it to favour his Bolivian site.
outcome.evidence: I see the principal flaw with the list is that it is built on the assumption that all of what Plato wrote is factual and not mythological and does not contain any errors or embellishments.

replies.what: Expanded the list by 26 criteria to 50 and applied it to 24 theories (as described by Atlantipedia).

sources.title: George Pararas-Carayannis, paper abstract for the Milos conference

searches.notes: Dates 11 to 13 July 2005 come from the Pararas-Carayannis conference paper abstract (drgeorgepc.com), which I fetched. The 24 criteria as listed by Atlantipedia say Atlantis was 'greater than Libya and Anatolia and Middle East and Sinai (combined)', not Plato's 'Libya and Asia'. I read all 24 as Atlantipedia prints them; the list is its transcription and the proceedings volume was not seen.

searches.title: Geology of the Richat Structure (Matton et al.)
searches.method: Field geology of the breccia, ring dykes and sediments of the dome, to explain how it formed.

announced.text: The structure is a Cretaceous alkaline complex that domed the rocks and was hollowed by hot-water karst, with erosion forming the rings.
announced.where: paper, Geology 33 (2005)
announced.evidence: The circular Richat structure and its breccia core thus represent the superficial expression of a Cretaceous alkaline complex with an exceptionally well preserved hydrothermal karst infilling at its summit.

outcome.text: The IUGS listed it in 2022 among 100 geological heritage sites as 'a spectacular example of a magmatic concentric alkaline complex'. This is a geology paper, not an Atlantis test; it sets the age and origin that Atlantis proposals must answer.
outcome.evidence: In respect of it being "a spectacular example of a magmatic concentric alkaline complex", the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS) included the Richat Structure in its assemblage of 100 geological heritage sites around the world, in October 2022.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Natural geology and age: a Cretaceous dome far inland, not a built or recently drowned site.

sources.title: Crossref record and abstract, Matton et al. 2005

searches.notes: Coordinates 21.1147 N, 11.3943 W from the Wikipedia page. The paper is not about Atlantis. The 40 km diameter and Late Proterozoic to Ordovician rocks are from the abstract and Wikipedia.

searches.title: Radiocarbon dating of the Thera eruption
who: Walter Friedrich and colleagues (Friedrich et al.)
Sturt Manning and colleagues (Manning et al.)
searches.method: Radiocarbon wiggle-matching of tree-ring segments of an olive tree buried alive by the tephra, and Bayesian analysis of 127 short-lived samples across the Aegean.

announced.text: The eruption dates to 1627 to 1600 BCE (95.4% probability), a century before the date from traditional Egyptian chronology. Manning's team put it in the late 17th century BCE.
announced.where: two papers, Science, 28 April 2006
announced.evidence: constrain the eruption date to the range 1627-1600 B.C. with 95.4% probability. ... it is a century earlier than the date derived from traditional Egyptian chronologies.

outcome.text: The date moved about a century earlier than archaeology had held, but stays about 8,000 years after Plato's. The Egyptian-linked chronology remains debated among archaeologists, per the search summaries I saw; I did not read the debate itself.
outcome.evidence: Radiocarbon (carbon-14) data from the Aegean Bronze Age 1700-1400 B.C. show that the Santorini (Thera) eruption must have occurred in the late 17th century B.C.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Direct radiocarbon dating of an olive branch buried by the eruption.

sources.title: Crossref abstract, Friedrich et al., Science 2006
Crossref abstract, Manning et al., Science 2006

searches.notes: The 8,000 years gap is my arithmetic. A 2018 Antiquity supplement (seen in search results only) says the calibration is sensitive to assumptions; not read.

searches.method: Marine geophysical study of salt tectonics and mud volcanism, published in Tectonophysics 470 (2009). Survey dates not seen.

searches.title: The 'Atlantis' grid in Google Ocean

place.name: About 600 miles (970 km) off northern Africa, near the Canary Islands

searches.method: A grid of straight lines in the Google Ocean sea-floor layer was read as streets. The layer mixed ship sonar depths with satellite-derived depths.

data.name: Atlantis_Ship_Tracks.kmz (Sandwell and Smith)
data.note: Link as printed by PCWorld, 24 February 2009; not fetched. Related catalogue id: srtm15-plus.

announced.text: A tabloid asked 'Is This Atlantis?' and quoted an aeronautical engineer saying the grid must be man-made.
announced.where: British tabloid, February 2009, reported by TechCrunch on 20 February 2009
announced.evidence: A British tabloid ran a boldfaced headline: "Is This Atlantis?" and quoted an aeronautical engineer as saying, "It must be man-made."

outcome.text: Google said the lines were the tracks of a survey ship. In 2012 a data update removed the grid, and Sandwell explained a velocity error on one grid-pattern survey cruise.
outcome.evidence: The particular cruise that created the 'Atlantis' problem was a systematic mow-the-lawn type survey in a regular grid pattern, so the resulting depth errors looked like a regular grid.

replies.what: "The lines reflect the path of the boat as it gathers the data."
Some squares are about 8 miles long, about 50 times a New York block; the pattern would vanish in the next Google Earth.
"Of course it is nonsense, but in a way brings public attention to the deep ocean."

searches.check_that_settled_it: A published explanation from the data's makers, and the corrected 2012 data layer.
searches.notes: Distances: TechCrunch says 620 miles west of Morocco near the Canary Islands, ABC says about 600 miles off northern Africa. No coordinates in the sources. Gizmodo called Google's first explanation 'dubious' (search result only); the 2012 Scripps account is the stronger one. The tabloid is named only by TechCrunch.

searches.title: Freund's 'Finding Atlantis' at Doñana
searches.method: Ground-penetrating radar, electrical resistivity tomography, magnetometers and spectrometers across the marsh, with radiocarbon dating.

announced.text: The team said it found a communal oven and canal systems buried in the park, evidence of a roughly 4,000-year-old civilisation flooded by a tsunami, and suggested the site was Atlantis and also the biblical Tarshish.
announced.where: National Geographic Channel film 'Finding Atlantis', broadcast 13 March 2011
announced.evidence: Scientists say they have found proof of a 4,000-year-old civilization that was buried by a tsunami.

outcome.text: Members of the Spanish team working there since 2005 criticised the claim. Their own results point to a third-millennium BCE settlement. Critics note the dates and size do not fit Plato.
outcome.evidence: Other researchers criticized the results, however, including members of a Spanish team who have been studying the site since 2005.

replies.what: "Richard Freund was a newcomer to our project and appeared to be involved in his own very controversial issue concerning King Solomon's search for ivory and gold in Tartessos" (quoted from the Telegraph by Colavito; the Telegraph piece was not fetched).
Says initial radiocarbon dates put the site at 5,000 to 2,400 years old, and that Plato's island was larger than Libya and Asia together.

sources.title: Jason Colavito, review of 'Finding Atlantis', 14 March 2011

searches.notes: An Atlantipedia profile of Villarías-Robles (search result, not fetched) says Freund offered geophysics help in 2009. Colavito's page is a personal blog. I did not see the film or any paper by Freund, and the Telegraph article was not available, so Freund's own words are not quoted. The film also covered a 'carved shield' map claim per Colavito.

searches.title: Jimmy Corsetti's Richat video ('Bright Insight')
searches.method: A video argument comparing the Richat's rings with Plato's description of the city, as summarised by Novella; the video was not fetched.

announced.text: Per neurologist and sceptic Steven Novella: the Richat's concentric rings match Plato's city, and the Atlanteans built into the natural dome.
announced.where: online video, 2018 (summarised in a NeuroLogica Blog post of 19 November 2018)
announced.evidence: Jimmy admits that it is a natural structure, but gets around this massive problem by simply claiming that the Atlantians built their city into the natural formation.

outcome.text: Nobody has reported excavating for a city at the site. The dome's origin is settled geology. Novella notes there is no archaeology of a city there.
outcome.evidence: there is absolutely no evidence of a city in the Richat structure 12,000 years ago.

replies.what: Calls the video 'crank pseudoscience' and says the rings are a general match, not a specific one.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Natural geology (Matton et al., 2005): an eroded Cretaceous dome.

sources.title: NeuroLogica Blog, 'No - Atlantis Has Not Been Discovered in North Africa'

searches.notes: I did not watch or fetch the video, so I do not quote Corsetti himself. The date comes from the Novella post. Corsetti also discussed it on a podcast (search result only, not fetched).

searches.title: Merlin Burrows: 'towers' and a sea wall at Doñana
searches.method: Satellite images and surveys to find 'large circles', a sea wall and what the company called early concrete, with samples taken.

announced.text: The company said it had found remains of temples and towers and a long sea wall, with material thought to be early concrete dated to 10,000 to 12,000 years. A film titled 'Atlantica' was announced.
announced.where: press interviews (Live Science, quoted by BGR, 28 November 2018)
announced.evidence: Dating of the material, which is thought to be early concrete, suggested it was between 10,000 and 12,000 years old, which would fit the rough timeline of when Atlantis is said to have existed.

outcome.text: A critic found the oval 'circles' were experimental ponds dug in 2004 to 2005 for a zooplankton study, and that they are absent from older Google Earth imagery. The ponds' construction is confirmed by the published paper.
outcome.evidence: As part of the restoration, a set of experimental ponds was excavated in Caracoles estate (Fig. 1 and [35]) between 2004 and 2005. This experimental pond area ... contains 96 elliptically-shaped temporary ponds

replies.who: A Hot Cup of Joe (archaeologist blog, 2019)
replies.what: Says the circles disappear if you move the Google Earth timeline back, and that the company later withdrew links to 'Towers of Poseidon' claims. Blog author unnamed in the text I read.

searches.check_that_settled_it: Earlier satellite imagery plus the published description of the pond experiment (Frisch et al., PLoS ONE 2012).

sources.title: BGR, 'High-Tech Search Company Claims To Have Discovered Atlantis', 28 November 2018
A Hot Cup of Joe, 'How the Discovery of Atlantis Made Big News Then Faded Away'
Frisch et al., PLoS ONE 7(7): e40205 (2012)

searches.notes: I confirmed from the PLoS paper that 96 elliptical ponds were excavated in Caracoles estate between 2004 and 2005, at 37 07 N, 6 31 W. surveyors Sergio and Alejandro Aleu Ruiz
